turn_text: Thank you. So speaking of that kind of compromise, one of your signature legislative achievements was authoring and passing the No Child Left Behind Act, which obviously bolstered education standards and expanded the federal government's reach into education. Could you talk about what it was like in those negotiations between you and Senator Kennedy and how interest groups and other groups influenced how that process went?

Well, this is a classic example of the way the government worked when I was there. Senator Kennedy was the lion of the left of the liberals. He was the dominant force in America for many years in defining the liberal agenda. He was chairman of the Health Education Labor and Pension Committee. I was ranking, or at this time I was second in seniority on that committee. And George W. Bush came into office as a president who intended to focus on domestic issues. Unfortunately, 9-11 changed all that. But up until 9-11, he was very much focused in that direction. And one of his priorities was to try to improve elementary and secondary education, because He and I think most Americans recognized our public school system wasn't working very well as a general statement and worked well with some specifics. And so the first thing he did was gather leaders in the House and the Senate for a gathering. It was a small gathering in Texas even before he was sworn in to try to lay the groundwork for reaching an agreement on a major piece of legislation which would hopefully address that issue. And as a result of that, Senator Kenney and myself, Congressman Boehner, who wasn't speaker at the time, was Chairman of the Education Committee in the House, and George Miller, who was the ranking Democrat on that committee, who was from Oakland, we met for four or five months, every week. And negotiated very aggressively what we thought we needed. First, we had hearings and we got some background on what people were thinking generally. But we went into very specific negotiations. We were joined by Margaret Spelman, who was President Bush's Secretary of Education. But it was every day, every week, a couple of times a week, and it was intense. I mean, we had intense disagreements, but the difference, and we reached an agreement finally, on a fairly significant piece of legislation, very significant at the time. The reason we reached agreement was because everyone in that room, all four of the players who were legislators, weren't there to shout, they were there to govern. We knew that we were going to have to reach compromise in order to govern. Senator Kennedy, who had the loudest voice in the room, was perfectly willing to govern. And so we did. And it took a long time to work out the details, but it ended up being a very good bill, in my opinion. Over the years, it got dissipated because it was such a good bill that both the left and the right hated it. The left hated the fact that it held teachers accountable and schools accountable, and the right hated the fact that it was a federal bill. But it was good law. And that's the way things worked if you were going to get things done. You had to come together. You know, any issue that's really complex in our society, and most public policy issues are complex if there are any significance. They do require compromise. And in the American system, nothing passes unless the American people feel it's fair. It will not get popular support unless it's deemed fair by the American people.
